stem: A checkout agent runs six scoped tools at a 0.4% misroute rate across 90,000 monthly requests. Product wants twelve general-purpose tools added "for flexibility," though logs show no request needs a capability outside the six. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Add the twelve tools, but restrict their availability to business hours to limit exposure.
Add one narrowly scoped tool for the cross-role lookup the logs show is missing.
Add the twelve tools and log every invocation so unnecessary use can be reviewed later.
Decline the addition; the six-tool surface already meets the workflow at no added token cost.

whyRight: The six scoped tools already cover every logged request pattern, so the requirement is already satisfied. Adding twelve general-purpose tools for unmeasured future flexibility pays a token cost on every request and reintroduces confusable neighbours without fixing anything the current metrics show is broken.

whyWrong.A: Restricting the new tools to business hours narrows a time window, not the tool count; the token cost and confusable-neighbour risk persist for every request the rest of the day.
whyWrong.B: The stem's own logs already show no request needs a capability the current six don't cover, so there is no missing cross-role lookup to build a tool for.
whyWrong.C: Logging invocations records unnecessary use after it already happened; it never prevents the token cost or the misroute risk the extra tools would add.

t1Clause: logs show no request needs a capability outside the six
lessonKey: added addition already cost decline meets six surface token tool workflow

stem: A reimbursement agent's daily approval capability needs provable audit logging under a new compliance mandate; its delete capability is never invoked. The team proposes a system-prompt line telling the agent to record its own actions. What should the architect implement instead?

opts.t: Remove the prompt-level logging instruction and rely on the model to self-police the delete capability.
Replace the prompt line with a more detailed, carefully worded self-reporting instruction for every action.
Remove the delete capability from the tool configuration, and log every approval call at the tool-invocation layer.
Keep both capabilities, and log every approval and delete call at the tool-invocation layer.

whyRight: The compliance requirement is proof of action, which a prompt instruction cannot guarantee since the model can omit or misreport it. Enforcing the log at the tool-invocation layer makes it deterministic, and removing the never-used delete capability closes the actual privilege gap.

whyWrong.A: Dropping the logging instruction abandons the proof-of-action requirement entirely, and self-policing does nothing about the delete capability still sitting unused in the configuration.
whyWrong.B: A more detailed instruction is still a prompt-level self-report the model can skip or misstate; the audit mandate needs proof, not better wording.
whyWrong.D: The scenario states the delete capability is never invoked; logging it does not close the actual gap, which is an unneeded privilege still sitting in the configuration.

t1Clause: its delete capability is never invoked
lessonKey: approval call capability configuration delete every invocation layer log remove tool

stem: A risk-classification service faces a regulator-mandated p95 latency SLA of 2,000ms that cannot be relaxed, currently met with no slack. Compliance also wants a 6-point accuracy gain, but every available accuracy lever adds latency. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Add a self-critique pass for the full accuracy gain, and request a one-time exception to the regulator SLA.
Apply the cheapest accuracy-per-millisecond lever that fits the SLA, accept a smaller gain, and report the shortfall.
Switch to a larger generation model for the full gain, since the SLA has margin to absorb it.
Reduce retrieved chunks to free latency budget for a reranking stage that reaches the full gain.

whyRight: The SLA is regulator-mandated and cannot be relaxed, and no accuracy lever is free, so the only defensible move is the cheapest lever that stays inside the budget, taking a smaller accuracy gain and reporting the remaining shortfall honestly to the business.

whyWrong.A: The scenario states the SLA cannot be relaxed; requesting an exception discards the one constraint that is fixed to fully satisfy the one that is negotiable.
whyWrong.C: The stem states the SLA is already met with no slack; a larger model adds latency the budget does not have to absorb.
whyWrong.D: Cutting retrieved context removes something the workflow requires and usually loses more accuracy than a reranking stage would recover in this budget.

t1Clause: the SLA is regulator-mandated and cannot be relaxed
lessonKey: accept accuracy apply cheapest fits gain lever millisecond per report shortfall sla smaller

stem: A support request passes through an intake agent, a triage tool, and a specialist agent across 40,000 tickets a day, each logging under its own request ID. Diagnosing a wrong answer requires reconstructing the full path. What should the architect implement?

opts.t: Instrument tool calls and retrieved context at each hop, but keep each service's own separate request ID.
Propagate a single correlation ID from the intake agent through every downstream hop and tool call.
Add per-stage timing to each service's logs to see where the response spends time.
Have an engineer manually cross-reference timestamps across each service's logs to reconstruct the path.

whyRight: A request that crosses three separate services fragments into three disconnected logs unless one identifier ties every hop together. Propagating a single correlation ID from intake onward is the only option that lets engineers reassemble the full path a specific wrong answer actually took.

whyWrong.A: Richer per-hop instrumentation still leaves three separate request IDs; the trace still cannot be reassembled into one path across services.
whyWrong.C: Per-stage timing diagnoses a latency regression, not a correctness problem; it says nothing about which hop caused the wrong answer.
whyWrong.D: Manual timestamp cross-referencing reconstructs by hand, per incident, what a correlation ID would have made automatic and repeatable at 40,000 tickets a day.

t1Clause: diagnosing a wrong answer requires reconstructing the full path
lessonKey: correlation every hop id one propagate through

stem: A stable RAG system's answer quality drops the same night a scheduled 40,000-document refresh completes with full re-index coverage and an unchanged chunking configuration. The refresh pipeline shows no errors. What should the architect investigate next?

opts.t: Re-run the refresh pipeline end to end, since the timing points to the ingestion job as the cause.
Lower the retrieval top-k so fewer, more targeted chunks reach the generation step.
Check whether the embedding model version changed in the same deployment window, independent of the refresh.
Add a manual review step where an analyst spot-checks degraded answers before they reach users.

whyRight: The refresh completed cleanly with full coverage and an unchanged chunking scheme, so it is a coincidence, not the cause. A version change to the embedding model in the same window would silently shift the vector space and degrade retrieval without any refresh-side error.

whyWrong.A: The stem already states the pipeline shows no errors and coverage is full; re-running it targets a cause the evidence has already ruled out.
whyWrong.B: Reducing top-k changes how many chunks reach generation, not which vector space they were matched against; it does not touch the actual cause.
whyWrong.D: Manual spot-checking catches degraded answers after users could see them; it diagnoses nothing about why retrieval degraded in the first place.

t1Clause: the refresh pipeline shows no errors
lessonKey: changed check deployment embedding independent model refresh same version whether window

stem: Applying the principle that a present-but-poorly-ranked document calls for reranking rather than added depth, a support-search system's correct document sits at rank 11 of 20 candidates on 92% of matching queries. What should the architect implement?

opts.t: Raise top-k from 20 to 50 so the correct document is captured further down the list.
Replace the retrieval mechanism with a different embedding model to improve match quality.
Add a reranking stage that reorders the existing top-20 candidates before passing the top few into context.
Lower the generation temperature so the model weighs the top-ranked chunk more heavily.

whyRight: The correct document is already inside the candidate set on 92% of matching queries; the failure is ranking, not absence. Reordering the existing top-20 with a reranking stage fixes exactly that, without the added tokens and latency a wider retrieval pass would cost.

whyWrong.A: The document is already retrieved; widening top-k floods context with lower-relevance chunks and adds cost without fixing where rank 11 sits.
whyWrong.B: Swapping the embedding model replaces a mechanism that is already surfacing the correct document, to solve a ranking problem it does not cause.
whyWrong.D: Temperature governs token sampling during generation; it has no effect on which candidate document the retrieval step ranked eleventh.

t1Clause: the correct document sits at rank 11 of 20 candidates
lessonKey: add candidate existing over reranking set stage

stem: A support-triage agent handles 5,000 requests a day from a knowledge library of 40 document categories that product expands almost monthly. It needs a standing sense of which categories exist, not a per-request decision to search. Which mechanism should represent the category list?

opts.t: Expose the category list as an MCP tool the agent decides whether to call each request.
Expose the category list as a read-only MCP resource the agent can consult as needed.
Hardcode the current 40 categories directly into the system prompt as static instructions.
Delegate catalog questions to a separate cataloguing agent the assistant hands off to.

whyRight: A read-only MCP resource gives the agent an always-available map of what exists without spending a model decision on every request, and it stays current as product adds categories, unlike a static instruction block or an extra hop through another agent.

whyWrong.A: A tool works only if the model chooses to call it on that turn, adding a decision and a round trip the agent doesn't need just to know what exists.
whyWrong.C: The stem states categories are added almost monthly, so a list frozen into the prompt goes stale within weeks and misrepresents what the library actually contains.
whyWrong.D: A dedicated agent brings its own judgment and accountability to a task that is only reading a list, adding a full inference hop where none is warranted.

t1Clause: it needs a standing sense of which categories exist, not a per-request decision to search

stem: Following progressive discovery principles, a research assistant's system prompt embeds the full text of a 900-entry document catalog, adding about 9,000 tokens to every request, even though most requests never reference the catalog at all. Which change best fits the principle?

opts.t: Replace the embedded text with an MCP resource the agent queries only when a request actually needs the catalog.
Replace the full catalog text with a shorter summary paragraph kept in the system prompt on every request.
Remove the least-referenced entries from the catalog so the remaining list fits comfortably in the prompt.
Keep the full catalog embedded but enable prompt caching to cut the repeated token cost.

whyRight: The catalog is background awareness the agent rarely needs, not content every request requires, so progressive discovery applies: expose it as a resource fetched on demand. That removes the fixed 9,000-token tax from requests that never touch the catalog, exactly what the principle calls for.

whyWrong.B: A shorter summary still sits in the system prompt on every request, so the fixed per-request cost shrinks but never disappears.
whyWrong.C: Deleting entries removes required capability rather than fixing how the catalog is presented, and the agent becomes unaware of documents that still exist and may be needed.
whyWrong.D: Caching is the right fix when identical content is needed on every request; here most requests never touch the catalog at all, so caching preserves an unnecessary cost.

t1Clause: most requests never reference the catalog at all

stem: A scheduling assistant handling 50,000 requests a day only books and cancels calendar events. Designers keep twelve extra tools 'for flexibility': eleven are never called, and one runs a cross-role lookup used on nearly every turn. Which statement best evaluates this tool set?

opts.t: Remove all twelve tools, including the cross-role lookup, since none are part of the core booking and cancellation workflow.
Keep all twelve, but write clearer descriptions so the eleven idle tools are easier to tell apart.
Log usage on all twelve for a quarter, then decide later which ones to prune.
Remove the eleven unused tools; keep the twelfth as a scoped cross-role tool since it runs on nearly every turn.

whyRight: Eleven tools sit idle yet still tax every request in tokens and add confusable neighbours; only the twelfth earns its place because it is a narrowly scoped, genuinely high-frequency cross-role lookup -- the sanctioned exception, not blanket 'flexibility.'

whyWrong.A: Removing every tool discards the one sanctioned exception: a narrowly scoped, genuinely high-frequency cross-role lookup earns its place even under a strict removal policy for idle tools.
whyWrong.B: Clearer descriptions help once the decision space is already small; they don't remove the eleven idle tools' fixed token cost or blast radius.
whyWrong.C: Logging records afterwards that eleven tools sat unused; it doesn't stop them from taxing every request or widening blast radius until the quarter ends.

t1Clause: one runs a cross-role lookup used on nearly every turn

stem: A multi-tenant assistant retrieves from a tiered, query-filterable store under one shared account; auditors require enforcement provable at the point of access. A teammate proposes a system-prompt rule naming which tiers the agent may cite instead. Select two best next steps.

opts.t: Propagate the requesting user's identity into the retrieval query so entitlement is enforced before ranking.
Add a post-retrieval review step that removes restricted results before the answer is shown.
Reject the system-prompt rule; access control needs deterministic enforcement, not an instruction the model might not follow.
Split the store into separate indexes per entitlement tier, even though the current store already filters at query time.

whyRight: Both hold: entitlement must be enforced at the query itself, since anything filtered later already reached context and traces, and the enforcement must be deterministic -- a system-prompt rule is a probabilistic instruction, not access control auditors can point to as proof.

whyWrong.B: A second review pass filters restricted content after it has already entered context and the trace store -- the exposure already happened by the time review catches it.
whyWrong.D: Splitting indexes is the answer only when the store cannot filter at query time; here it already can, so this adds infrastructure the situation doesn't need.

t1Clause: the vector store can filter at query time

stem: A shared pipeline serves a live chat widget, where users read answers as they arrive, and a nightly reconciliation job processing 40,000 records that only parses the complete response, measured against a p95 total-latency SLA. Streaming is enabled across the pipeline. Which change is correct?

opts.t: Enable streaming more aggressively on the reconciliation job too, so both paths finish sooner.
Keep streaming only on the chat widget, and cut total latency at the reconciliation job's slowest stage.
Disable streaming across the whole pipeline and report the improved mean latency.
Give both paths one shared timeout budget tuned to the median request.

whyRight: The chat widget's users read incrementally, so streaming is worth keeping there; the reconciliation job waits for the complete response, so streaming buys it nothing -- the fix is to keep streaming for the interactive path and separately reduce total time in the batch path.

whyWrong.A: The reconciliation job parses only the complete response, so streaming changes nothing it can measure; it just adds complexity to a path streaming can't help.
whyWrong.C: A real change, but mean latency is not the SLA's metric; the p95 tail is what the contract names, and this doesn't show it moved.
whyWrong.D: The stated SLA is measured at p95, not the median; a budget tuned to the median request says nothing about the percentile the contract actually names.

t1Clause: a nightly reconciliation job ... that only parses the complete response
lessonKey: batch interactive only optimize path stream time total

stem: While designing the metrics backend for an assistant handling 300,000 requests a day, a teammate proposes labelling every metric with the calling user's ID so support can filter dashboards by individual customer. Which response is correct?

opts.t: Reject the proposal; keep user ID out of metric labels and serve per-user lookups from the trace store instead.
Skip the label; take a small uniform sample of routine metric events to spot-check customer patterns instead.
Redact the user ID field in metrics entirely so support loses per-customer filtering, but cardinality stays low.
Stand up a separate per-user metrics store, sharded by customer, so filtering doesn't affect the shared backend.

whyRight: Metrics need low-cardinality dimensions to stay fast and affordable; a user-ID label multiplies cardinality by every customer. Per-user slicing is a real need, but it belongs in the trace store, which already carries session and document identifiers at the individual-record level.

whyWrong.B: Uniform sampling of routine events builds a baseline distribution; it doesn't let support pull up records for one specific customer, which is the actual ask.
whyWrong.C: Redacting the field removes the cardinality problem by removing the feature itself; support still can't filter by the customer they were asked to look up.
whyWrong.D: A sharded per-user metrics store solves a cardinality problem the trace store already solves, at the cost of a second backend to build and operate.

t1Clause: so support can filter dashboards by individual customer
